snp5.4:1.1: Nd II explains the Buddha’s having “seen the roots” in three ways: (a) that greed, aversion, and delusion are the roots of the unskillful, while their absence roots the skillful — citing AN 6:39, though Nd II’s quotation there adds phrasing not found in the sutta itself, apparently to close off the implication that good or bad destinations could exist beyond the deva, human, and lower realms; (b) that all unskillful qualities are rooted in ignorance (per SN 20:1) while all skillful qualities are rooted in heedfulness (per SN 45:79–80, SN 45:82, and SN 46:31); and (c) that ignorance is the root of all the factors of dependent co-arising. For a further sense in which the Buddha saw the root, see MN 1.
snp5.4:1.6: A similar question receives a different answer at Sn 3:4.
snp5.4:4.5: On the question of rebirth in the suttas generally, see the essay The Truth of Rebirth.
snp5.4:6.4: Per Nd II, “evaporated” means that one’s misconduct in body, speech, and mind — together with all one’s defilements — has dried up and vanished.
snp5.4:6.5: Both AN 3:32 and AN 4:41 discuss this closing verse. In AN 3:32, Ven. Ānanda asks whether a monk could develop a concentration free of “I”-making, “mine”-making, or underlying conceit with regard to this body, to any external object of concentration, and within the release of awareness and discernment. The Buddha says yes, describing the perception behind it as: “This is peace, this is exquisite — the stilling of all fabrications, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the ending of craving, dispassion, cessation, unbinding” — and says the poem’s final verse was spoken with that state of mind in view. In AN 4:41, the Buddha names four ways of developing concentration — leading to a pleasant abiding in the present, to knowledge and vision, to mindfulness and alertness, and to the ending of the effluents — and says the final verse was spoken with these four in mind. Although the verse doesn’t name concentration directly, its phrase “nothing perturbing” seems to point to the “imperturbable” states of concentration; see MN 102, note 2, and MN 106, note 1.
